Berkshire Beats Challenge to $535 Million Talc Bankruptcy Deal — WSJ
data.description:
By Akiko Matsuda

A New Jersey bankruptcy judge approved a $535 million deal for Berkshire Hathaway and others to resolve asbestos-injury liabilities tied to a defunct affiliate, rejecting claims the deal negotiators were conflicted.

Judge Michael Kaplan of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Trenton, N.J., on Thursday ruled against representatives for asbestos-injury claimants who challenged the proposed settlement between affiliates of Berkshire Hathaway and its former talc supplier Whittaker Clark & Daniels.

The judge said the settlement represents "by far the surest pathway to securing a timely, fair and reasonable recovery for all creditors" and rejected claims that independent directors who hammered out the terms were conflicted due to their business ties to law firm Kirkland & Ellis, Whittaker's bankruptcy counsel.

Whittaker filed for bankruptcy in 2023 to resolve mounting lawsuits from personal-injury claimants who alleged asbestos-containing talc made its way into consumer products like Old Spice powder and Mary Kay cosmetics. Once in bankruptcy, Berkshire negotiated the $535 million settlement with independent directors a Berkshire executive appointed to the Whittaker board.

Representatives for tort claimants alleged the number was too low to compensate current and future asbestos claims and the disinterested directors were conflicted because they received referrals on other matters from Kirkland & Ellis. Companies on the brink of insolvency often appoint independent directors referred by their law firms to handle dealings with its owners and affiliates and mitigate conflict-of-interest concerns.

The Whittaker claimant representatives alleged independent directors generally "are compromised and incentivized by the possibility of future employment to produce an outcome that is favorable to the entity that appointed them," a criticism that has also been leveled in other chapter 11 cases.

But, while Whittaker's directors had received referrals from Kirkland before, Kaplan in his ruling found no evidence of "undue influence over the execution of their duties" or that they were beholden to the firm. The judge said a settlement between Berkshire and Whittaker alone would be viewed as an insider transaction, but the presence of the independent directors had severed the insider ties.

Suzanne Ratcliffe, a lawyer representing mesothelioma victims with claims against Whittaker Clark, said Thursday's ruling is wrong.

"Whittaker Clark & Daniels must be held accountable for poisoning people to death with asbestos in our nation's civil justice system," Ratcliffe said. "Instead, this order blesses a greed-fueled insider 'settlement' between Whittaker and multibillionaires — including Berkshire Hathaway affiliates — a settlement which no victim wants or asked for."

Representatives for Whittaker and Kirkland didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

For more than a century, Whittaker supplied pigments and minerals, including talc, for cosmetic and industrial products. In 2004, the company, then a subsidiary of German railroad operator Deutsche Bahn, sold its operating assets, including its long-held talc distribution assets, to subsidiaries of Brenntag North America. Whittaker then became a shell entity managing legacy asbestos liabilities.

In 2007, Berkshire Hathaway's insurance arm, National Indemnity, acquired Whittaker's equity and assumed its asbestos liabilities, insurance policies, and roughly $129 million in cash from Deutsche Bahn for a nominal $1, court papers show. The acquisition was part of Berkshire's property-casualty insurance business, in which Berkshire invests the premiums until it is required to pay claims.

But a recent surge in lawsuits alleging asbestos exposure through cosmetic talc products has since upended that business model. Berkshire said in 2023 that bankruptcy would provide a fairer and more efficient way of addressing over 1,600 pending talc lawsuits.

The $535 million settlement was negotiated between Whittaker on one side and Brenntag, Deutsche Bahn and Berkshire on the other. The contributing companies agreed to fund the settlement in exchange for being released from asbestos-related liabilities stemming from their past involvement with Whittaker.

Lawyers representing personal-injury claimants have challenged the proposed deal, which they argue undervalues their claims. Their experts estimated the value of claims at as much as $5.3 billion, while Berkshire's experts said the value would be less than $520 million.

In a separate ruling, Judge Kaplan approved Whittaker's $16.5 million environmental settlement with federal and state regulators, clearing a final regulatory hurdle to the company's chapter 11 plan. Funded by National Indemnity, that agreement resolves legacy pollution claims across five sites in California and Montana, including a Superfund site in Billings.

Write to Akiko Matsuda at akiko.matsuda@wsj.com

data.title: Novartis U.S. Shares Fall After MS Pill Trial Data Disappoint
data.description:
By Adria Calatayud

Novartis's U.S. shares fell after the Swiss drugmaker reported results of two late-stage studies of its multiple sclerosis pill that showed a reduction in flare-ups below that achieved by a rival drug from Roche Holding.

American depositary receipts in Novartis fell as much as 4.5% in U.S. midday trading Friday before recovering somewhat, reducing their year-to-date gains.

Novartis said its drug, known as remibrutinib and marketed as Rhapsido for skin condition chronic spontaneous urticaria, met the primary goals of the studies by reducing relapse rates relative to Sanofi's rival treatment Aubagio in patients with relapsing MS, the most common form of the disease. The results were presented at scientific congress MSToronto2026 in Toronto and published in medical journal the Lancet.

The studies showed the drug achieved reductions in the annualized relapse rate of 35.2% and 31.2% compared to Aubagio, the company said. This translated into one relapse every 13 years, it added.

No liver safety signal was observed, Novartis said.

Novartis, which was recently hit by trial failures of cholesterol and neuromuscular drugs, already reported initial findings from the studies last month, but analysts said a look at the full data was required to assess how its drug performed against the competitor product from Roche.

Roche, Novartis's Swiss cross-town rival, previously said its own multiple sclerosis pill, fenebrutinib, lowered the annualized relapse rate by 51.1% and 58.5% in two late-stage studies, but its drug showed signs of potential liver injury.

Analysts at UBS had said before Novartis released the full study data that the company would likely need to deliver efficacy data at least on par with Roche's fenebrutinib with a clean safety profile to trigger a positive market reaction.

Novartis said there were no cases that would raise concerns about drug-induced liver injury in its trials. Roche reported a case of potential liver damage.

By combining high efficacy with a favorable safety profile, the medicine has the potential to support long-term disease management, Novartis Chief Medical Officer Shreeram Aradhye said.

Write to Adria Calatayud at adria.calatayud@wsj.com

data.title: First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows
data.description:
Key points:
  • Tanker with 40,000 tons of diesel bound for New York
  • Expected to arrive on November 7
  • First US imports of Russian petroleum product since 2022 ban
  • Russia to send initial 300,000 tons to US, global markets -Trump
  • Buyer and seller not known yet

The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.

Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US midterm elections.

Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.

The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia's Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7.

The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.

Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter".

A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.

"As far as I'm aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.

The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.

RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTS

Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.

It also supplies Central Asia by rail.

Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.

It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, LSEG data showed.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.

Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia's sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.

That account was not accurate, a source familiar with the matter said.

Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.

data.title: Siacoin Improved Storage Reads in SDK v0.13.2
data.description:
Siacoin updated Sia Storage SDK for Rust to v0.13.2. The version makes storage reads more reliable when host lists or connection conditions change.

Refer to the official tweet by SC:

Sia Foundation
@SiaFoundation

Storage reads are now more dependable across changing host listings and connection conditions in Sia Storage SDK (Rust) v0.13.2.

Explore the developer portal at 🔗 https://t.co/rVc4FcPOfv.

Oct 23, 2026

SC Info

Sia serves as a trustless and secure marketplace for cloud storage, where users can rent out their unused storage space. The primary objective of Sia is to position itself as the backbone storage layer of the internet, aiming to compete with major cloud storage providers like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft by offering more competitive storage rates due to its decentralized nature.

In the Sia network, files are divided into 30 encrypted segments, each stored with a different host for redundancy purposes. The relationships between those who upload and those who host files are governed and enforced through smart contracts on Sia’s blockchain. Siacoin facilitates transactions within this network, with renters paying hosts in SC for storage services, and hosts using SC as collateral within these smart contracts to ensure reliability and trust.

Siacoin (SC) is the native utility token of Sia, a decentralized cloud storage platform built on blockchain technology. Siacoin has an unlimited supply to match the potentially limitless demand for data storage and transactions on the network. New Siacoins are minted as mining rewards via a proof-of-work algorithm, with the mining reward now fixed at 30,000 SC per block. The introduction of The Sia Foundation has led to a doubling of the block reward, with half going to the Foundation. Siacoins are removed from circulation when hosts forfeit their tokens due to bad actions. The Sia team plans to implement a proof-of-burn mechanism where hosts must burn a portion of their earnings to demonstrate their legitimacy. The Sia development team pre-mined approximately 30 million SC before public release, but the team and investors hold less than 0.1% of the total Siacoin supply.

data.title: Democratic midterm sweep could be bad for AI, good for healthcare, EPFR says
data.description:
Key points:
  • Dow falls >1%, S&P 500 dips, Nasdaq edges down
  • Staples weakest S&P 500 sector; just energy, tech rise
  • Dollar, bitcoin gain; US crude rises >3%; gold dips
  • US 10-year Treasury yield rises to ~4.99%

DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM SWEEP COULD BE BAD FOR AI, GOOD FOR HEALTHCARE, EPFR SAYS

Investors are worried that a Democratic sweep in next month's US midterm elections could be a headwind for artificial intelligence and the data center sector but could be supportive for healthcare and infrastructure, according to EPFR.

A Democratic "blue wave" is viewed by some investors as a potential headwind for AI-related companies and data center operators, which could face stricter environmental requirements, greater local opposition to projects and proposals requiring developers to shoulder more of their power-related costs. A Republican-controlled Congress, by contrast, is generally seen as more supportive of rapid AI deployment and data center expansion, EPFR said.

Still, EPFR fund flows data suggests investor enthusiasm for AI and data centers remains intact. Its data centers & AI infrastructure funds attracted inflows for the 12th time in the past 13 weeks and for the 27th time in the past 32 weeks. AI-focused funds saw inflows in 26 of the past 27 weeks as AI companies continued to support the broader US stock market.

The prospect of Democratic gains highlights sectors that could benefit from increased government support, including healthcare, infrastructure and clean energy, according to EPFR. Democrats have traditionally backed healthcare spending as well as large-scale infrastructure projects, including public transit, power-grid modernization, and renewable-energy facilities.

However, investors have yet to embrace clean-energy funds, according to EPFR data. Its clean energy funds recorded their 17th outflow in the past 20 weeks, with redemptions rising to an 11-week high. Electric vehicle funds posted outflows for the 16th time in 24 weeks, with redemptions hitting a 37-week high.

data.title: Korea and Taiwan Built Economies on AI. One Failed IPO Shows Their Fragility. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By William Pesek

South Korea and Taiwan have become the world's ultimate AI trade. Their exports, investments, stock markets and increasingly their economic fortunes hinge on the assumption that the world's appetite for AI infrastructure will keep accelerating.

If that assumption fails, the fallout will reach well beyond Silicon Valley. But the first issue will be the impact on the 74 million people who call Korea and Taiwan home. If AI has a Wile E. Coyote moment in which investors look down, see nothing beneath their portfolios, and sell hard, the Seoul and Taipei markets will likely lead the world in financial carnage.

Korea especially. It has moved fastest and most boldly to mold its economy around AI. Ask Koreans last January what their economy's lifelines were and most would have said cars, ships, smartphones, or K-pop. Today, the universal answer is AI, for better or worse.

Chips now make up 41% of Korean exports, which jumped 83.5% year-over-year in September. Semiconductor shipments surged 263% and computer exports rose 435% on an annual basis. Despite import tariffs, exports of semiconductors to the U.S. climbed 137%. One of Korean President Lee Jae Myung's main pledges before taking office in June 2025 was to double the Korea's blue-chip index, the Kospi, to 5,000. The AI boom delivered on that promise that quickly.

That boom is starting to look fragile, however. An ominous sign came on Tuesday, with Elice's dismal initial public offering in Seoul. Shares in the AI cloud and business software provider plunged 32% on its opening day, showing how much investors doubt the payoff of the vast capital the firm is pouring into the AI buildout.

Elice made its debut on the tech-heavy Kosdaq, but the Kospi is a cautionary tale in its own right. It remains above the 5,000-level Lee promised, and its 31% gain this year is impressive. Yet it is far below its all-time high of 9,385 in June. Few investors had a top-12 economy's stock market trading like a meme stock on their 2026 bingo cards.

This moment carries important warnings for the new Korean economy. The country's nominal gross domestic product surged 26.4%, year-over-year in the second quarter — the fastest pace in nearly 47 years (recall the late-1970s heyday of the "Asian tigers"). Some key sectors of the economy have seen triple-digit gains, month after month. It is hard to characterize that type of explosive growth as healthy or sustainable for a developed, $2.25 trillion economy.

The scale of AI-driven growth puts the Bank of Korea in a tough position. On Thursday, the central bank left interest rates unchanged at 3%, opting to wait and see the effects of two previous rate hikes this year. But with Korea arguably the most leveraged bet on AI anywhere, the bank's policy parameters might have to shift in real time.

The BOK's policy will have to strike a perfect balance, using the blunt instrument of rates to tame inflation in Korea's "old economy" without killing the golden goose that replaced that old economy growth engines just 12 months ago. Complicating matters, Korea doesn't know when or where exactly an AI reversal could originate, whether from a shock at home or abroad.

Taiwan presents a similar story. When economists warn about the concentration of AI hardware production in major Asian economies, they are really talking about the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

On paper, TSMC directly drives as much as 15% of Taiwan's roughly $1 trillion in annual economic output. The indirect boost it provides the economy is almost incalculable, but it includes roughly 1,600 domestic suppliers who rely on TSMC.

TSMC also makes up at least 42% of the Taiwan Stock Exchange Weighted Index, and its boom is the main reason the bourse has rallied 62% this year. That leaves the market hypersensitive to any forward guidance from TSMC CEO C.C. Wei and his team. An AI correction could trigger a sharp reversal in Taiwan's blistering 12.9% year-over-year growth rate in the second quarter, which is the fastest since 1987.

History may well smile on Lee and Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te for betting so heavily on AI. Both are holding winning lottery tickets, at least for now. Of course, Samsung, SK Hynix, and TSMC didn't pioneer this revolution, and their spoils owe as much to being in the right place at the right time as to any special foresight.

Still, their two economies now risk entering a tech version of the "resource curse." Oil, diamonds, and other underground riches too often warp incentives, let governments neglect other lucrative industries, and distort economies. AI spoils are propelling Seoul's property values skyward, for example. And worries about AI turbocharging the gap between Korea's haves-and-have-nots has prompted Lee to roll out a $1 trillion-plus plan to spread the benefits to the country's less prosperous regions.

If an AI-stock downturn takes hold beyond the market drop this week, Korea's heavy reliance on AI could pose a threat to the global financial system. At the start of the 1997 Asian financial crisis, Korea's economy was worth roughly $600 billion. It is now 3.7 times that.

Korea and Taiwan's AI bets look brilliant when capital keeps pouring in. But when entire economies are built on a single trade, the difference between a growth miracle and financial pain can be just one earnings disappointment or failed IPO away.

Guest commentaries like this one are written by authors outside the Barron's newsroom. They reflect the perspective and opinions of the authors. Submit feedback and commentary pitches to ideas@barrons.com.

William Pesek is a longtime Asia opinion writer, based in Tokyo. He is a former columnist for Barron's and Bloomberg and the author of Japanization: What the World Can Learn from Japan's Lost Decades.

data.title: SEC Exams Division Eyes Private Credit, Complex Financial Products in 2027 — Market Talk
data.description: The SEC Division of Examinations says it will continue to monitor the development of illiquid or less-liquid investments, including private credit, and complex financial products as part of its 2027 priorities. The division highlights risks around valuation, redemptions, conflicts of interest, and disclosures. It also plans to examine "novel or complex investment strategies, including in funds with leverage vulnerabilities, such as BDCs [business development companies] and inverse and leveraged ETFs, and RICs [registered investment companies] that operate in reliance on exemptive orders, including their implementation and compliance with such orders," the division says. It adds that it will continue to prioritize RICs which haven't been previously examined. (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)
